title: California Attorney General Serves Investigative Subpoena on OpenAI
content:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta yesterday served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of the California Department of Justice’s (DOJ) ongoing investigation of incidents resulting from the operations of OpenAI and its artificial intelligence (AI) models. Last month, Attorney General Bonta announced that DOJ is conducting a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident, while continuing to more broadly monitor the AI industry’s compliance with California laws. The subpoena is part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.
“My office is asking OpenAI additional questions regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its AI models,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Frontier models can be legitimate tools for cyber defense — at the same time, companies that develop these models and offer them for use have a moral and legal responsibility to ensure that they do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks, either during model testing and development or once models are placed into service. Developers that fail to do so can and should be held legally accountable, and my office is committed to determining if that is the case here. As the top law enforcement official of California, I am committed to using all the tools at my office's disposal to keep California’s residents safe.”
DOJ encourages anyone with information regarding this, or any similar cybersecurity incidents or risks, to contact oag.ca.gov/report.
Attorney General Bonta is committed to ensuring that AI is safe for both users — including children and teens — and the public. Last month, he and a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general sent a letter to Congress to urge leaders to take immediate action to regulate large scale AI models and developers, in light of recent reports of critical cyber safety incidents at multiple frontier AI labs and warnings from insiders that the continued pace of AI development is becoming increasingly dangerous. In January, he announced opening an investigation into reports of rampant nonconsensual sexually explicit material on X and produced using Grok, an AI model developed by xAI. DOJ also stands ready to enforce California's recently enacted companion chatbot children's safety (SB 1119) and chatbot-enabled toy (SB 867) laws when they become effective.
Last year, Attorney General Bonta issued two legal advisories reminding Californians of their rights and advising businesses and healthcare entities that develop, sell, or use AI of their obligations to comply with existing California laws. He also sent a letter to 12 of the top AI companies after reports of sexually inappropriate interactions between AI chatbots and children. Attorney General Bonta has time and time again defended California's right to protect residents from risks posed by AI technology. He is proud to have opposed the federal government's first, second, and third attempts to prevent state regulation of AI, and remains committed to defending California’s laws amid the Trump Administration's attempts to hobble states' right to protect their residents and foster safe AI technology.

report.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI, expanding a state probe into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving its AI models.
report.background: California has become a leading state-level regulator of AI, and OpenAI is headquartered in San Francisco, making it a natural target. The subpoena follows a formal California DOJ investigation announced last month into the Hugging Face incident and broader monitoring of AI industry compliance. It also comes amid growing concern over frontier model cyber capabilities, child safety, and chatbot harms. Bonta recently joined bipartisan attorneys general urging Congress to regulate large-scale AI models, opened an investigation into nonconsensual sexual material linked to xAI's Grok, and warned 12 top AI companies about inappropriate chatbot-child interactions. California's new companion chatbot and chatbot-toy laws add enforcement teeth. The action reflects escalating state-federal tension over AI oversight.
key_points: Subpoena and scope: Bonta served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of a California DOJ investigation into incidents and risks from OpenAI's operations and AI models. The probe focuses on cybersecurity incidents and risks. The subpoena seeks additional answers, signaling the inquiry is escalating beyond voluntary information requests and could lead to enforcement action.

Legal theory: Bonta said frontier models can aid cyber defense, but developers have moral and legal duties to prevent their models from perpetrating or enabling cyberattacks during testing, development, or deployment. Companies that fail can and should be held legally accountable. This frames AI security as a consumer-protection and public-safety issue.

Broader enforcement pattern: California DOJ is investigating the Hugging Face incident, monitoring AI compliance, probing Grok/X over nonconsensual sexual content, and preparing to enforce SB 1119 and SB 867 on companion chatbots and toys. Bonta also sent legal advisories and a letter to 12 AI companies about child safety.

Federal-state conflict: Bonta and bipartisan AGs urged Congress to regulate frontier AI, citing cyber safety incidents and insider warnings. California has opposed three federal attempts to block state AI regulation and vows to defend state laws against Trump administration preemption efforts. The subpoena is part of that state-rights enforcement strategy.
report.impact: For AI developers, the subpoena raises the stakes on security documentation, model testing, red-teaming, incident disclosure, and post-deployment monitoring. OpenAI and peers may face more state-level investigations, especially where models could enable cyber misuse or harm minors. Startups could see compliance costs rise, while larger labs may accelerate safety teams and legal reviews. For users, the probe could lead to stronger safeguards, age verification, and faster takedowns of harmful outputs, but also slower feature rollouts or stricter access. For the industry, it signals that state attorneys general are becoming de facto AI regulators, creating a patchwork of rules even as federal preemption fights continue.
report.tools: To follow AI security and compliance, watch California OAG's AI enforcement page, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, MITRE ATLAS, and OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Open-source tools include Microsoft PyRIT for red-teaming, NVIDIA Garak for LLM vulnerability scanning, promptfoo for eval testing, and Llama Guard or NeMo Guardrails for safety filtering. The AI Incident Database and OECD AI Incidents Monitor track real-world harms.
